discrepancies.bridge: The formal declarations cover only coefficient types carrying a commutative-ring structure. The blueprint gives an ordered family indexed by `1,…,k` and does not state that `K` is commutative (or even explicitly impose a ring structure). stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-cor.fps.lim.justification: Both elaborated signatures impose `∀ {K : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing K]`, whereas the blueprint says only “Let k ∈ ℕ” and then asserts the sum and the ordered product `∏_{i=1}^k f_{i,n}`, without requiring that `K` be a commutative ring. The arbitrary `Finset ι` quantification is otherwise more general than the source's `{1,…,k}`, and the two target declarations together supply both conjuncts. The definitions of `CoeffStabilizesTo` and `Seq.StabilizesTo` exactly match the blueprint's coefficientwise eventual stabilization.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-cor.perm.re.justification: All three formal theorems match the corresponding clauses. For (a), `∀ ... (σ τ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)), (σ * τ).length % 2 = (σ.length + τ.length) % 2` is exactly the natural-number remainder formulation of `ℓ(στ) ≡ ℓ(σ)+ℓ(τ) (mod 2)`. For (b), `(σ * τ).length ≤ σ.length + τ.length` directly matches `ℓ(στ) ≤ ℓ(σ)+ℓ(τ)`. For (c), `Word n = List (Fin (n - 1))` encodes a sequence `k₁,…,k_q ∈ [n-1]`, `wordProd w = (List.map simpleTransposition w).prod` encodes `σ = s_{k₁}⋯s_{k_q}`, and the conjunction `List.length w ≥ (wordProd w).length ∧ List.length w % 2 = (wordProd w).length % 2` gives both claimed conclusions. The definitions also agree: `length σ = σ.inversions.card`, with inversions `{p | p.1 < p.2 ∧ σ p.2 < σ p.1}`, and permutation multiplication satisfies `(σ * τ) x = σ (τ x)`, as required. Using `Fin n` and `Fin (n-1)` instead of the one-based sets `[n]` and `[n-1]` is a faithful index re-encoding; the formal simple transposition swaps the corresponding adjacent positions.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint’s primitive subtraction axiom can be recovered routinely from the additive-group structure supplied by `[inst : Ring R]`: Lean subtraction is addition of the negative, and additive cancellation gives `a + b = c ↔ a = c - b`. Conversely, the blueprint axiom determines subtraction as addition of an additive inverse. Thus the displayed unary-negation law is an equivalent standard re-encoding, but it does not itself state the required binary-subtraction equivalence.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.alg.rin.justification: All addition, multiplication, identity, distributivity, and annihilation axioms are represented with the correct orientations, and omission of multiplication commutativity agrees with “the ‘Commutativity of multiplication’ axiom is removed.” The sole mismatch is that the blueprint explicitly requires a binary map `\ominus : K×K→K` satisfying “`a⊕b=c` if and only if `a=c⊖b`,” whereas the corresponding target only asserts `∀ ... (a : R), a + -a = 0`. The `[inst : Ring R]` binder supplies the additive-group structure needed to derive the omitted equivalence, so this is a routine representational bridge rather than a substantive divergence.

discrepancies.bridge: There is no bridge from uniqueness of elements satisfying `a * b = 1` to the blueprint’s two definitional clauses. The theorem neither characterizes an inverse as an element satisfying both `a * b = 1` and `b * a = 1`, nor defines invertibility/unit status as existence of such an inverse. Recovering those clauses would require introducing definitions absent from the formal declaration; they are not consequences supplied by this uniqueness theorem.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.commrin.justification: The formal declaration asserts only `a * b = 1 → a * c = 1 → b = c`, i.e. uniqueness of two right inverses. The blueprint instead states definitions: “An inverse ... of `a` means an element `b∈L` such that `ab=ba=1`” and “`a` is invertible ... if `a` has an inverse.” Although commutativity makes `ab = 1` imply `ba = 1`, the formal theorem still does not state either requested definition or the existential notion of invertibility.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.cyclele.justification: The target unfolds to `σ.cycleType`. The supplied characterization of `Equiv.Perm.cycleType` is exactly “the multiset of lengths of the non-trivial cycles of a permutation; fixed points contribute nothing and every member is ≥ 2,” matching the informal definition: “the multiset of lengths of the nontrivial cycles (length ≥ 2) in the cycle decomposition of σ.” The binders `[Fintype α]` and `[DecidableEq α]` respectively encode the stated finite setting and the computational equality structure needed by the formal definition.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.dcdlist.justification: The body `(List.map List.formPerm cycleReps).prod` maps every input list to its cycle permutation and composes the resulting permutations. For a list of distinct entries `[a₁, …, aₖ]`, `List.formPerm`, defined as `(List.zipWith Equiv.swap l l.tail).prod`, sends `a₁ → a₂ → … → aₖ → a₁` and fixes all other elements, matching the informal definition of `cyc_{a₁,…,aₖ}`. The outer `List.prod` uses permutation multiplication characterized by `(σ * τ) x = σ (τ x)`, exactly matching the blueprint convention that `αβ = α ∘ β`. The binder `[DecidableEq α]` is only the computational encoding needed to construct swaps, while `Equiv.Perm α = α ≃ α` correctly represents permutations as bijections.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint places no algebraic hypothesis on `K`, whereas the formal theorem applies only when `K` is a commutative ring. There is no uniform bridge to the statement as written: for an arbitrary `K` the displayed operations may not exist, and even under a broader ring interpretation the supplied `Matrix.det` is restricted to commutative rings. Recovering a determinant statement outside that setting would require specifying additional structure and potentially defining and proving a different result.

Relabel the textbook index set `[n] = {1,…,n}` by `Fin n = {0,…,n-1}` using the bijection `i ↦ i+1`. Transporting the matrix and conjugating each permutation along this bijection preserves its sign and relabels the finite product and sum, yielding the textbook formula.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.det.det.justification: The elaborated signature requires `∀ {K : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing K]`, while the blueprint only says “Let `A ∈ K^{n × n}`” and calls the result an element “of `K`,” without fixing `K` to be a commutative ring. Under the package rule that an omitted setting cannot be assumed, this is a substantive restriction. Independently, the formal matrix is `(A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) K)` and permutations range over `Equiv.Perm (Fin n)`, while the blueprint explicitly uses `[n] = {1,2,…,n}` and `S_n`; these indexings are routinely equivalent by relabeling. The formal `Equiv.Perm.sign σ • …` otherwise matches the blueprint’s integer sign `(-1)^σ` acting on the product: the supplied docstring identifies `Equiv.Perm.sign` as `1` for even and `-1` for odd permutations.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.finsets.justification: The package does not define the informal notation `[n]` or specify whether its elements are `0,…,n−1` or `1,…,n`. The formal side uses `Fin n`, whose elements are natural numbers strictly below `n`, and `finsetSumFin` has body `fun {n} P => ∑ i ∈ P, ↑i`. If `[n] = {0,…,n−1}`, all three definitions directly match the blueprint: `imageFinset` is the image under a permutation, `permsMapping` filters all permutations by that image equality, and `finsetSumFin` is the stated subset sum. If `[n] = {1,…,n}`, the sum under the natural correspondence `i ↦ i+1` would instead be `∑ i ∈ P, (↑i+1)`, so the formal sum differs by `|P|`. A definition of `[n]` (or an explicit indexing convention) is therefore needed to decide faithfulness.

discrepancies.bridge: For an arbitrary coefficient type K, represent an FPS exactly as the blueprint does, by a function a : ℕ → K, and define its n-th coefficient to be evaluation a n. Then the claimed equality is immediate by unfolding. Thus extending the coefficient definition beyond commutative rings requires only a routine re-encoding, not the substance of a new proof.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.coe.justification: The formal signature restricts coefficients to `∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing R]`, whereas the blueprint defines an FPS merely as a sequence `(a_n)_{n∈ℕ} ∈ K^ℕ` and states `[x^n] a := a_n`, without imposing any algebraic structure on K. Subject to the formal encoding, `(PowerSeries.coeff n) (PowerSeries.mk a) = a n` exactly expresses recovery of the n-th sequence entry, so there is no further discrepancy.

discrepancies.bridge: The formal definition can be instantiated only when `K` is a commutative ring. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.div.justification: The elaborated signature quantifies `{K : Type u_1} → [inst : CommRing K]`, whereas the blueprint says an FPS over `K` is a sequence `K^ℕ` and states only that `a₀ = 0`; neither informal definition imposes a commutative-ring structure on `K`. discrepancies.bridge: The formal equivalence applies only when the coefficient type carries a commutative-ring structure. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.fps.justification: The blueprint says an FPS over K “means a sequence ... ∈ K^ℕ of elements of K,” with no hypothesis on K. The elaborated signature instead begins `{R : Type u_1} → [CommRing R] → PowerSeries R ≃ (ℕ → R)`. discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint’s condition only needs an FPS viewed as a sequence, a distinguished element `1 ∈ K`, and equality: it is simply the equation `a₀ = 1`. The formal definition restricts this to commutative rings because `PowerSeries.constantCoeff` is exposed as a ring homomorphism. For a more general coefficient type, one can routinely define the same predicate by directly evaluating the underlying sequence at degree zero; on commutative rings this is exactly `PowerSeries.constantCoeff f = 1`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.has.justification: The defining equation is faithful: the target body is `PowerSeries.constantCoeff f = 1`, matching the blueprint’s “`[x^0]f=1`,” and `PowerSeries.constantCoeff` is documented as “The constant coefficient of a formal power series.” However, the elaborated signature requires `[CommRing K]`, while the informal statement and supplied FPS definition quantify over coefficients in `K` without fixing `K` to be a commutative ring. This is a routine scope restriction rather than a substantive mathematical mismatch. Representing the condition as the proposition `HasConstantTermOne f` instead of literal set-membership notation `f ∈ K[[x]]₁` is only a notational re-encoding.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.inf.justification: After unfolding the alias and dependencies, the formal definition is `∀ m ≤ n, ∀ (J : Finset I), M ⊆ J → coeff m (∏ i ∈ J, a i) = coeff m (∏ i ∈ M, a i)`. This exactly matches the blueprint’s requirement that `M` determine the product’s `x^m`-coefficient for every `m ∈ {0,1,…,n}`. A `Finset I` already represents a finite subset of `I`, so the informal condition `J ⊆ I` is inherent in its type. `PowerSeries.coeff m` is the stated `m`-th coefficient, and the alias merely swaps the argument order.

After unfolding the body, the target is exactly `fun p m => {ik | ik.2 ≠ 0 ∧ (PowerSeries.coeff m) (p ik.1 ik.2) ≠ 0}`. This matches the blueprint’s set `T_m = { (i,k) : k ≠ 0 and [x^m] p_{i,k} ≠ 0 }`: `ik.1` and `ik.2` are respectively `i` and `k`, while `PowerSeries.coeff m` is documented as the `m`th coefficient. The formal `PowerSeries K` representation is a one-variable formal power series, agreeing with the informal sequence definition. The target docstring’s mention of finiteness is not part of the declaration body and is not claimed by the informal definition.

The target body is exactly `fun ... p n => {i | ∃ k, (i, k) ∈ PowerSeries.CoeffSupportSetUnion p n}`, matching the blueprint’s `I_n = { i ∈ I : ∃ k, (i,k) ∈ T'_n }`. Unfolding `PowerSeries.CoeffSupportSetUnion` gives `⋃ m ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), PowerSeries.CoeffSupportSet p m`; since `Finset.range (n + 1)` consists of `0,…,n`, this is precisely the stated `T'_n = T_0 ∪ T_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ T_n`. Unfolding `PowerSeries.CoeffSupportSet` also agrees with the supplied definition of `T_m`, namely `k ≠ 0 ∧ [x^m] p_{i,k} ≠ 0`.

After unfolding the target, `PowerSeries.ValueSetKn p n = {k | ∃ i, (i, k) ∈ PowerSeries.CoeffSupportSetUnion p n}`, exactly matching the blueprint’s `K_n = { k ∈ ℕ : ∃ i, (i,k) ∈ T'_n }`. Moreover, `CoeffSupportSetUnion` is `⋃ m ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), CoeffSupportSet p m`, i.e. the union over precisely `m ≤ n`, matching `T'_n = T_0 ∪ ⋯ ∪ T_n`; and `CoeffSupportSet p m` is `{ik | ik.2 ≠ 0 ∧ coeff m (p ik.1 ik.2) ≠ 0}`, matching the stated definition of `T_m`. The arbitrary index type `I` and commutative-ring formal setting do not weaken the claimed definition.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint definitions make an FPS merely an element of `K^ℕ`, and coefficientwise stabilization uses only indexing and equality, so they apply without a commutative-ring structure on `K`. The formal definition only applies when `[CommRing K]` is available. Recovering the blueprint for an arbitrary coefficient type would require introducing a separate `ℕ → K` representation and redefining coefficientwise stabilization; an arbitrary type cannot in general be equipped with a commutative-ring structure.

The omitted uniqueness assertion follows routinely: if the coefficients of a sequence eventually equal those of both `f` and `g`, then for each `n`, choose the two stabilization bounds and evaluate at their maximum to obtain `coeff n f = coeff n g`; extensionality of formal power series then gives `f = g`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.lim.justification: The formal signature restricts the coefficient type via `{K : Type u_1} → [CommRing K]`, whereas the blueprint defines an FPS simply as “a sequence ... in `K^ℕ`” and its stabilization definition only requires equations `a_i = a`; no algebraic assumption on `K` is fixed in the supplied statement or those definitions. Thus the formal domain is strictly narrower. Separately, the formal body asserts only `∀ n, Seq.StabilizesTo ...`, while the blueprint additionally says: “This is legitimate, because `f` is uniquely determined by the sequence.” That uniqueness is absent from the declaration, though it is an immediate consequence of its predicate.

discrepancies.bridge: The formal definition chooses one stabilization bound N and uses the coefficient of the partial product through N, whereas the blueprint says the coefficient agrees with every sufficiently large partial product. From PowerSeries.IsMultipliable, all factors with index i ≥ N have coefficients equal to those of 1 through degree n. Hence adjoining any such factor does not change the n-th coefficient; induction over the finite tail shows that every partial product with sufficiently large endpoint has the same n-th coefficient as the chosen one. Thus the choice-based implementation recovers the blueprint's choice-independent formulation.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.lim.justification: The blueprint says the n-th coefficient equals `[x^n](∏_{j=0}^{N} f_j)` “for any sufficiently large N.” The formal body instead sets it to `(PowerSeries.coeff n) (∏ j ∈ Finset.range (N + 1), f j)` for a single `N := ⋯.choose`. The range correctly represents j = 0,…,N, and `PowerSeries.IsMultipliable` exactly matches the stated multipliability condition, but independence from the selected sufficiently large N is not itself expressed by this declaration. It follows by the routine stabilization argument described in the bridge.

discrepancies.bridge: The formal definition can only be instantiated when the coefficient type carries a `CommRing` structure. The blueprint does not impose commutative-ring axioms on `K`; its coefficientwise finite sum needs only suitable zero and additive structure. Recovering the blueprint at that stated generality would require constructing the sum anew for those more general coefficient types, rather than specializing this declaration. In particular, no `CommRing K` instance can be derived from the supplied informal definitions.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.lim.justification: The target begins `{K : Type u_1} → [inst : CommRing K] → ...`, whereas the blueprint says simply that a summable family of FPSs has coefficients `∑_{i ∈ S_n} [x^n] f_i`. Its FPS definition permits sequences in `K^ℕ`, and none of the supplied informal definitions states that `K` is a commutative ring. Apart from this restriction, the bodies agree: `PowerSeries.IsSummable f` is exactly finiteness of `{i | coeff n (f i) ≠ 0}`, and `tsum'` forms each coefficient by summing over that set's `toFinset`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.log.justification: The target body is `PowerSeries.mk fun n => if n = 0 then 0 else (algebraMap ℚ K) ((-1) ^ (n - 1) / ↑n)`, but the package provides neither the signature nor the body/docstring of `PowerSeries.mk`. Consequently, it is unavailable whether `PowerSeries.mk f` constructs the FPS whose coefficient of `x^n` is `f n`. That fact is essential to compare the body with the blueprint’s `∑_{n≥1} ((-1)^{n-1}/n) x^n` and its asserted constant term `0`. The definition of `PowerSeries` alone as `MvPowerSeries Unit` does not determine this constructor’s indexing behavior.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.mul.justification: Unfolding the body, the coefficient of the output at `m` is `↑((m + fun₀ | i => 1) i) * (MvPowerSeries.coeff (m + fun₀ | i => 1)) f`. Here `fun₀ | i => 1` is the standard basis exponent `e_i`, and evaluation at `i` gives `(m + e_i) i = m i + 1`. Thus this is exactly the informal coefficient `(m_i + 1) · a_{m + e_i}`. The result is bundled as `MvPowerSeries σ R →ₗ[R] MvPowerSeries σ R`, matching “This defines an `R`-linear map.” The `[DecidableEq σ]` binder is implementation data needed for the finitely supported standard basis vector, and `[CommSemiring R]` supplies the coefficient and linear structures used by the statement.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint imposes no stated algebraic assumptions on K, whereas all five formal declarations are restricted to commutative rings. The coefficient formulas themselves are definitional componentwise/convolution formulas and extend routinely to the weaker structures needed to interpret the individual operations (in particular, commutativity is unnecessary; they hold over an ordinary possibly noncommutative ring). Reproving them there is an unfolding-level bridge rather than a substantive new argument.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.ops.justification: Every elaborated signature contains the binder `[inst : CommRing R]`, while the blueprint only says that an FPS is a sequence “in K^N” and directly defines sum, difference, scalar multiplication, product, and constants without stating that K is a commutative ring. Apart from that restriction, the formulas match exactly: addition and subtraction are coefficientwise; scalar multiplication gives `c * coeff n f`; `Finset.antidiagonal n` is documented as the pairs `(i,j)` with `i+j=n`, matching the convolution in (d); and `PowerSeries.C a` has coefficient `a` at zero and zero otherwise, matching (e). The representation `PowerSeries R = MvPowerSeries Unit R`, with `MvPowerSeries σ R = (σ →₀ ℕ) → R`, is a routine re-encoding of a sequence indexed by ℕ when σ is Unit. The use of `PowerSeries R` also re-encodes the notation K[[x]], and a constant series can be expressed as one of the form `PowerSeries.C a`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.pol.justification: The decisive part of the definition is hidden. The blueprint requires “the truncation of f at the degree bound given by Lemma … degree-bound,” namely an N satisfying “[xⁿ]f = 0 for all n ≥ N.” The formal body is `(fun N => (PowerSeries.trunc N) f) ⋯.choose`, but the package does not expose the proposition proved by `⋯`. From the displayed term alone, `⋯.choose` could choose from any existential over ℕ, so it is impossible to verify that the selected N is a degree bound rather than an unrelated natural number. The available definition `FPS.IsPolynomial f := {n | PowerSeries.coeff n f ≠ 0}.Finite` correctly matches the informal polynomial condition, but that does not determine the omitted witness construction. The package would need to show the type of `⋯`, ideally `∃ N, ∀ n, N ≤ n → PowerSeries.coeff n f = 0`, or an equivalent degree-bound lemma application.

discrepancies.bridge: The formal declarations only define and establish composition when the coefficient type is a commutative ring. The supplied blueprint never states that K is a commutative ring; its definitions use arithmetic operations but do not impose the CommRing axioms or commutativity. Recovering the unrestricted blueprint claim would therefore require either an additional source hypothesis that K is a commutative ring or a new construction and proof over every coefficient structure admitted by the blueprint. Neither follows from these declarations.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.sub.justification: All three elaborated signatures impose `[inst : CommRing K]`, including `fps_comp : ... [inst : CommRing K] → ...`, while the informal statement merely says “Let f and g be two FPSs in K[[x]]” and none of the supplied informal definitions fixes K to be a commutative ring. Settings absent from the package cannot be assumed. Apart from this restriction, the formal content matches the blueprint: `PowerSeries.constantCoeff g = 0` represents `[x^0]g = 0`; `fps_comp` unfolds to `PowerSeries.subst g f`; and `fps_comp_coeff_finite` gives the stated sum over `Finset.range (n + 1)`, namely d = 0 through n.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint does not impose commutativity of multiplication, or even explicitly require a commutative-ring structure, on `K`. Its summability condition and essentially finite coefficientwise sum only require enough additive structure to form finite sums; even all the listed FPS operations remain meaningful over a noncommutative ring. The formal declarations only cover `R` carrying `CommRing R`. Recovering the blueprint for other admissible coefficient systems cannot be done by specialization or a consequence of these declarations; the definitions would have to be generalized and their construction re-established under weaker assumptions.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.sum.justification: Both formal declarations impose the binder `[CommRing R]` (the second displays `[inst : CommRing R]`). By contrast, the blueprint says only that an FPS is a sequence in `K^ℕ` and defines summability by finiteness of `{i ∈ I | [x^n] a_i ≠ 0}`; none of the supplied informal definitions states that `K` is a commutative ring. Apart from this restriction, `SummableFPS f := ∀ n, {i | coeff n (f i) ≠ 0}.Finite` exactly matches “for each n, all but finitely many i ...”, and `summableFPSSum` uses `finsum` coefficientwise, which agrees with the blueprint on the finite supports guaranteed by summability.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint imposes no algebraic assumptions on `K` beyond using distinguished elements `0` and `1`, whereas both formal declarations apply only to commutative rings. For a blueprint coefficient type having `0` and `1` but no `CommRing` structure, define the sequence directly by `a i = if i = 1 then 1 else 0`; the two required coefficient equations follow immediately by splitting on `i = 1`. Thus recovering the unrestricted sequence-level definition is routine, although it is not a specialization of these formal theorems.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.x.justification: The informal definition says an FPS over `K` is merely a sequence in `K^ℕ`, and the statement specifies `(0,1,0,…)` without requiring that `K` be a commutative ring. In contrast, the elaborated signatures begin respectively with `∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing R]` and assert the coefficient equations only under that hypothesis. Apart from this restriction, `(PowerSeries.coeff 1) PowerSeries.X = 1` and `i ≠ 1 → (PowerSeries.coeff i) PowerSeries.X = 0` exactly match the blueprint’s two coefficient conditions; `PowerSeries` as `MvPowerSeries Unit R` is a routine encoding of a one-variable coefficient sequence.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint defines an FPS as an arbitrary sequence of elements of K and its equivalence relation uses only coefficient equality; no algebraic structure on K is fixed. The Lean definition applies only when the coefficient type carries a CommSemiring instance. Recovering the blueprint for coefficient types without such a structure is impossible from this declaration; one would need a new definition using sequences, or a coefficient operation requiring no semiring structure.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.fps.xne.justification: The formal signature restricts coefficients via `{R : Type u_1} → [CommSemiring R] → ...`, whereas the blueprint says an FPS is a sequence `K^ℕ` and defines equivalence solely by `each m ∈ {0,1,...,n} satisfies [x^m]f = [x^m]g`, without imposing any structure on K. Within the restricted commutative-semiring setting, the body `∀ m ≤ n, (PowerSeries.coeff m) f = (PowerSeries.coeff m) g` correctly expresses agreement of exactly the first n+1 coefficients, but it does not certify the unrestricted blueprint definition.

discrepancies.bridge: The body only defines the finite-support predicate. Recovering part (b) would require an additional definition of the infinite sum and a statement that, for an essentially finite family, it equals the finite sum over the nonzero indices. Nothing in this declaration mentions or constructs a sum, so that content cannot be obtained merely by unfolding it.

Part (a) itself only needs a distinguished zero. The same definition extends routinely to any `[Zero K]` by using `(Function.support f).Finite`; indeed, the referenced canonical `EssentiallyFinite` already has exactly that generality. Thus removing the commutative-ring restriction is a direct re-encoding rather than a new substantive proof.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.infsum..justification: The formal body is only `fun {R} [CommRing R] {ι} f => EssentiallyFinite f`, which unfolds to `(Function.support f).Finite`, exactly matching part (a)'s condition that `“the set { i ∈ I | a_i ≠ 0 } is finite”`. However, the informal statement also asserts in part (b) that `“the infinite sum ∑_{i∈I} a_i is defined to equal the finite sum ∑_{i∈I; a_i≠0} a_i”`; the target contains no sum or equality and therefore omits that entire clause. In addition, the formal binder `[CommRing R]` is stronger than the structure required by the finite-support definition, while the blueprint states the definition for elements of `K` without imposing that restriction.

discrepancies.bridge: Clause (c) permits an element of an arbitrary, possibly noncommutative, ring. The finite sum `∑ i ∈ Finset.range n, a ^ i` only needs the ordinary semiring structure underlying such a ring, so the same body can be re-encoded directly without assuming commutative multiplication.

For a possibly noncommutative ring, re-encode the source's explicitly ordered product `[1]_a [2]_a ⋯ [n]_a` as an ordered list/range fold rather than `Finset.prod`, whose supplied signature requires a commutative monoid. This is a routine representation change; alternatively, the factors are all polynomials in the single element `a` and hence commute.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-def.pars.qb.justification: The defining formulas themselves match: `qInt` has body `∑ i ∈ Finset.range n, q ^ i`, exactly the terms `q^0+⋯+q^(n-1)`, and `qFactorial` has body `∏ i ∈ Finset.range n, qInt (i + 1) q`, exactly `[1]_q⋯[n]_q`. Their polymorphism also covers the polynomial interpretation by choosing the polynomial ring and its indeterminate. The only mismatch is clause (c), which says “if `a` is an element of a ring `A`,” while the informal definition of “ring” explicitly allows noncommutative multiplication, but both elaborated signatures require `[CommSemiring R]`. Recovering the excluded cases requires only the direct finite-sum formula and an ordered-product re-encoding.

discrepancies.bridge: Prove that the family `k ↦ 1 - PowerSeries.X ^ (k + 1)` is multipliable in the Pi topology. The omitted generality is recovered by a one-line application of congruence to each coefficient equality, so the discrepancy is minor.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint imposes no commutative-semiring axioms on K: its FPS and x^n-equivalence definitions only require sequences, coefficient extraction, and equality. To cover an arbitrary K (including a noncommutative semiring or a coefficient type with no semiring structure), one cannot instantiate the formal theorem. One must instead reprove the monotonicity statement directly by restricting coefficient agreement from indices ≤ n to indices ≤ m. Although elementary, that is the entire substance of this theorem rather than an ancillary boundary case.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.fps.xne.justification: The formal relation is restricted at its root by `PowerSeries.XnEquiv : {R : Type u_1} → [CommSemiring R] → ...`, and the target correspondingly quantifies `∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : CommSemiring R]`. By contrast, the blueprint says only that an FPS over K is a sequence in `K^ℕ`, defines equivalence by coefficient equalities, and states: “Let m,n∈ℕ with m≤n. If f ≡[x^n] g, then f ≡[x^m] g.” None of the supplied informal definitions assumes that K is a commutative semiring. Thus the formal theorem proves the claim only for a restricted class of coefficient types, and recovering the unrestricted blueprint claim requires reproving the theorem outside that class.

The formal theorem states exactly that from `(a ≡[x^n] b)` one obtains `∀ (k : ℕ), a ^ k ≡[x^n] b ^ k`, matching “if … $a\overset{x^n}{\equiv}b$, then $a^k\overset{x^n}{\equiv}b^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.” Unfolding `PowerSeries.XnEquiv` gives `∀ m ≤ n, coeff m f = coeff m g`, exactly the informal requirement for every $m\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}$. `PowerSeries R = MvPowerSeries Unit R` is the standard one-variable formal-power-series encoding, and the `CommSemiring R` assumption supplies the Cauchy-product and natural-power operations required by the statement.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint does not impose any algebraic structure on the coefficient set K for this statement: an FPS is defined simply as a sequence in K, and x^n-equivalence only compares coefficients by equality. The formal theorem is restricted to coefficients in a commutative semiring because `PowerSeries.coeff` is packaged as a linear map. For an arbitrary K, the omitted case is recovered routinely by viewing FPSs as sequences and, for each m ≤ n, composing the equalities `[x^m]f = [x^m]g` and `[x^m]g = [x^m]h` by equality transitivity.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.fps.xne.justification: After unfolding `PowerSeries.XnEquiv`, the conclusion and hypotheses exactly match the blueprint: `∀ m ≤ n, coeff m f = coeff m g`, corresponding to “each m ∈ {0,1,…,n} satisfies [x^m]f = [x^m]g.” However, the elaborated signature adds `[inst : CommSemiring R]`, while the supplied informal statement and definition describe `K[[x]]` as sequences of elements of K and impose no semiring hypothesis on K. This restriction is removable by the same immediate pointwise equality-transitivity argument, so the discrepancy is minor.

discrepancies.bridge: The formal theorem can be instantiated only when the coefficient type has a commutative-semiring structure. The blueprint does not impose that structure on K: its FPS definition only describes elements of K[[x]] as sequences in K^ℕ. To recover the unrestricted blueprint claim, one would have to supply an unmentioned CommSemiring structure on K or separately prove the truncation equivalence in the source's unrestricted sequence setting; neither follows from the formal theorem.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.fps.xne.justification: The elaborated signature begins `∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : CommSemiring R]`, whereas the blueprint says only “Let n∈ℕ. Two FPSs f,g∈K[[x]]…” and defines an FPS as “a sequence … ∈ K^ℕ,” without fixing K to be a commutative semiring. Thus the formal theorem certifies the equivalence only for a narrower, algebraically structured class of coefficient types.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint does not impose any algebraic structure on the coefficient type K; an FPS is defined simply as a sequence in K^ℕ, and this particular claim only uses equality of coefficients. Thus the formal theorem cannot be instantiated for an arbitrary coefficient type lacking a CommSemiring structure. The omitted cases are nevertheless recovered routinely by unfolding the blueprint definition: when n = 0, the condition for every m ∈ {0} is exactly equality of the zeroth coefficients, requiring no algebraic operations or laws.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.fps.xne.justification: The elaborated signature restricts coefficients via `∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : CommSemiring R]`, whereas the blueprint says only “Two FPSs f,g∈K[[x]]” and defines an FPS as a sequence `K^ℕ`, without fixing any structure on K. Apart from this restriction, unfolding `PowerSeries.XnEquiv` gives `∀ m ≤ 0, coeff m f = coeff m g`, which is precisely `[x^0]f = [x^0]g`; `PowerSeries.constantCoeff` denotes that constant coefficient. The Unit-indexed multivariate representation of `PowerSeries R` is the standard one-variable encoding and introduces no semantic difference.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.gf-ws.f.justification: The width conclusion matches exactly: the blueprint says “have width $1$ or $2$,” while the target concludes `n = 1 ∨ n = 2`. The supplied informal definitions also match the formal notions of rectangle, domino, and tiling. However, the blueprint package gives no informal definition of “faultfree” or “fault.” Consequently, it is impossible to compare that hypothesis with the formal body `n > 0 ∧ ∀ (k : ℕ), ¬ DominoTilingsZ.hasFault n T k`, where `hasFault` means `k > 0 ∧ k < n` and no horizontal domino straddles the line at `k`. An informal definition of fault/faultfree is needed to determine faithfulness.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.gf-ws.r.justification: The blueprint does not define either “a fault at position $k$” or “dominos lying in the left part.” The formal side fixes these as `k > 0 ∧ k < n ∧ ∀ d ∈ T.dominos, ...` in `DominoTilingsZ.hasFault`, and `∀ p ∈ d.toShape, p.1 ≤ ↑k` in `DominoTilingsZ.Domino.inLeftPart`. Thus it is underdetermined whether the informal phrase includes the strict interior restrictions `0 < k < n`, and whether its notions of straddling and left part coincide with these bodies. The package would need the blueprint definitions of “fault at position” and “left part” to decide faithfulness. Conditional on those meanings agreeing, the result type and body do exactly construct a `Tiling (Rectangle k 2)` from precisely the dominos of `T` satisfying `inLeftPart k`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.gf-ws.w.justification: The target states `TilingsHeight2.weightGenFun tilingsHeight2_isFiniteType = PowerSeries.mk fun n => ↑(Nat.fib (n + 1))`. Unfolding `WeightedSet.weightGenFun`, the left side is the FPS whose coefficient at `n` is the number of elements of `TilingsHeight2` of weight `n`; unfolding `TilingsHeight2`, these are tilings of `Rectangle n 2`, with weight equal to the width `n`. The right side is precisely the FPS with coefficient `f_{n+1}`, since `Nat.fib` satisfies `fib 0 = 0`, `fib 1 = 1`, and the stated Fibonacci recurrence. Thus it exactly certifies the informal claim that the weight generating function of `D` is `∑_n f_{n+1} x^n`.

discrepancies.root: the binders `have A := fun i => (-2 * ↑↑i, 0); have B := fun i => (2 * ↑↑i, 0)`
discrepancies.bridge: Under the endpoint convention in the blueprint, informal path number `i` corresponds to formal index `i - 1`. Thus the formal path at that index has endpoints `(-2(i-1),0)` and `(2(i-1),0)`, whereas the blueprint's final clause says that path `i` has endpoints `(-2i,0)` and `(2i,0)`. These cannot both hold; already for `k = 1`, the prescribed tuple endpoints are `(0,0)` while the claimed nested path runs from `(-2,0)` to `(2,0)`. No reindexing makes both blueprint fragments simultaneously true.

The formal conclusion establishes only that some unique non-intersecting path tuple exists. To recover the blueprint's identification of that tuple as the explicitly described nested paths, one must separately define those paths, prove their lists satisfy the Dyck arc relation and endpoint conditions, and prove pairwise vertex-disjointness; uniqueness can then identify them with the existential witness. That construction and non-intersection argument are substantive and are not asserted by the theorem's signature.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.cat.justification: The formal endpoints are indexed by `i : Fin k` as `(-2 * ↑↑i, 0)` and `(2 * ↑↑i, 0)`. The blueprint first specifies `A_i := (-2(i-1), 0)` and `B_i := (2(i-1), 0)` but later says “path `i` goes from `(-2i, 0)` ... to `(2i, 0)`,” creating a literal off-by-one conflict. Independently, the formal conclusion is only `∃! pt, pt.isNonIntersecting`, while the blueprint identifies the unique tuple as “the nested Dyck paths” with a prescribed route through `(0,2i)`; that identification is absent from the proposition.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.dyc.justification: The target unfolds to path-finiteness of the specific graph on `ℤ × ℕ` whose arcs are diagonal up/down steps: `v.1 = u.1 + 1 ∧ v.2 = u.2 + 1 ∨ ... v.2 + 1 = u.2 ∧ 0 < u.2`. The blueprint only says “Dyck digraph is path-finite” but supplies no definition of “Dyck digraph.” Its Dyck definition instead defines a “Dyck word,” while `def.lgv.lattice` defines a different graph on `ℤ²` with east and north steps. Thus the package does not determine whether the graph formalized by `LGV.dyckDigraph` is the graph intended by the informal statement. A blueprint definition of the Dyck digraph, or an explicit identification of it with the formal graph, is needed.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.no-.justification: The formal theorem exactly states the claimed emptiness result. Its hypotheses `LGV.xDecreasing A`, `LGV.yIncreasing A`, `LGV.xDecreasing B`, and `LGV.yIncreasing B` unfold to the four weak coordinate-ordering conditions in the blueprint. It quantifies over `σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin k)` with `σ ≠ Equiv.refl (Fin k)`, matching a non-identity element of `S_k` under the blueprint’s explicit `Fin k` reindexing convention. `LGV.permuteKVertex σ B` unfolds to `fun i => B (σ i)`, exactly the stated tuple `σ(B)`. Finally, `LGV.nipatSet A (LGV.permuteKVertex σ B) = ∅` says that there is no path tuple with the specified endpoints whose distinct component paths share no vertex, since `nipatSet` is `{pt | pt.isNonIntersecting}` and `isNonIntersecting` is the pairwise no-common-vertex condition. The supplied integer-lattice digraph has precisely the east and north arcs of the informal definition.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint assumes summability only on the punctured dependent family \(\overline S=\{(i,k):k\ne0\}\). The formal theorem instead requires summability of the entire family, including every term \(p_{i,0}=1\). For an infinite index type, the added family of constant terms need not be summable in a discrete coefficient ring, so the blueprint hypothesis cannot generally establish the formal hypothesis. Recovering the blueprint conclusion would require the substantive missing proof that handles the zero terms as multiplicative units rather than summands; it cannot be obtained by applying this theorem.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.multipl.justification: The informal context says: “Assume that the family \((p_{i,k})_{(i,k)\in\overline S}\) is summable (where \(\overline S=\{(i,k):k\ne0\}\)),” and the target statement works “under the same assumptions.” In contrast, the elaborated signature assumes `(Summable fun ik => p ik.fst ↑ik.snd)`, indexed over the full dependent sum, with no restriction `ik.snd ≠ 0`. Together with `(∀ i, p i 0 = 1)`, this demands summability of all the added unit series across `I`, which is not implied by punctured-family summability. The Lean `Multipliable` conclusion in the pointwise topology is otherwise an appropriate topological encoding of coefficientwise finite determination over discrete `K`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.di.justification: The blueprint says only “any function $f$” and does not specify its domain, codomain, or coefficient structure, while the elaborated signature fixes `(f : ℕ → ℕ)` and performs all sums and products in `ℕ`. The supplied commutative-ring definitions do not connect any ring `K` or `L` to this statement. Thus the package does not determine whether the intended claim is merely for natural-valued functions—under which reading the formal theorem matches—or for functions valued in an arbitrary commutative ring or another structure—under which reading the formal theorem would cover only a special case. A specification of the type of `f` and the intended arithmetic is needed.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.fi.justification: The formal theorem quantifies over `∀ (n m : ℕ)` and equates `{p | p.largestPart ≤ m}` with `Nat.Partition.restricted n fun x => x ≤ m`. Unfolding `restricted` gives exactly the partitions `x : Nat.Partition n` satisfying `∀ i ∈ x.parts, i ≤ m`. Unfolding `largestPart` gives `Multiset.fold max 0 p.parts`, the maximum of the parts with value `0` for the empty partition, matching the blueprint convention. Thus the two sides are precisely “partitions of n whose largest part is ≤ m” and “partitions of n with all parts ≤ m,” as claimed.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.perm.ik.justification: Unfolding `setQ`, the hypothesis `k ∈ σ.setQ i j` is exactly `i < k ∧ k < j ∧ σ j < σ k ∧ σ k < σ i`, matching the blueprint’s `k ∈ Q`. Unfolding `inversions` and finset difference, the conclusion says `(i,k)` is an inversion of `σ` and is not an inversion of `σ * Equiv.swap i j`. Since permutation multiplication satisfies `(σ * τ) x = σ (τ x)`, the latter permutation is precisely `σ ∘ t_{i,j}` as in the informal statement. Thus the formal conclusion exactly expresses that `(i,k)` is a lost inversion. Using `Fin n` rather than the one-based set `[n]` is a routine finite-order re-encoding and does not alter the claim.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.perm.su.justification: The left-hand side matches the blueprint: formal `∑ i, σ.lehmerEntry i` unfolds to the sum over `Fin n` of the cardinalities of `{j | i < j ∧ σ i > σ j}`, agreeing with `∑_{i ∈ [n]} ℓ_i(σ)` under the stated `Fin n` reindexing convention. However, the blueprint’s right-hand side merely says `ℓ(σ)` (“the length”) and the package supplies no informal definition of permutation length. The formal right-hand side unfolds through `Equiv.Perm.length` to `σ.inversions.card`, where `inversions` is `{p | p.1 < p.2 ∧ σ p.2 < σ p.1}`. Determining faithfulness therefore requires the missing informal definition of `ℓ(σ)`; one may not assume that it means inversion cardinality.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pie.moe.justification: The formal hypothesis `(∀ I ⊆ S, b I = ∑ J ∈ I.powerset, a J)` exactly represents the blueprint assumption `b_I = ∑_{J⊆I} a_J` for every `I⊆S`, since `I.powerset` is the finset of all subsets of `I`. Its conclusion `∀ I ⊆ S, a I = ∑ J ∈ I.powerset, (-1) ^ (I \ J).card • b J` exactly represents `a_I = ∑_{J⊆I} (-1)^{|I\setminus J|}·b_J`, with the coefficient computed in `ℤ` and `•` supplied by `Module ℤ A`. The binders `[AddCommGroup A] [Module ℤ A]` match the additive abelian group and integer-module setting. `Finset`, `[DecidableEq α]`, and defining `a b` on all finsets rather than only subsets of `S` are routine finite-set encodings and do not weaken the claimed result.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint allows “any K-algebra,” whose underlying ring may be noncommutative, while `FPS.polyEval` and hence the theorem require `A` to be a commutative ring. For an arbitrary noncommutative K-algebra, the claimed formula is nevertheless immediate from the blueprint definition `f[a] := ∑ₙ fₙ aⁿ`; equivalently, the same polynomial-evaluation expansion can be stated using `Polynomial.aeval`, whose supplied signature only requires `Semiring A`. Thus recovering the omitted cases is a routine generalization/unfolding, not a substantive new argument.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pol.eva.justification: The informal definition says, “Let A be any K-algebra,” and defines such an algebra using an underlying “(noncommutative) ring.” In contrast, the elaborated target contains `[inst_1 : CommRing A]`, inherited by `FPS.polyEval`, so it covers only commutative target algebras. Apart from that restriction, the conclusion exactly matches the blueprint: `FPS.polyEval f a = f.sum fun n c => (algebraMap K A) c * a ^ n`, where `Polynomial.sum` sums over `f.support`; the mapped coefficient multiplication represents the scalar term `f_n · a^n`.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint allows an arbitrary K-algebra A, whose underlying ring may be noncommutative. The formal definition FPS.polyEval, and consequently the theorem, is only available when A is a commutative ring. To recover the blueprint claim one must generalize polyEval to noncommutative rings (for example using Polynomial.aeval, which itself only requires a Semiring A with an Algebra K A structure) and prove the finite-support expansion in that generality. The stated theorem cannot itself be instantiated for a genuinely noncommutative A, so this requires a new generalized proof rather than a specialization.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pol.eva.justification: The blueprint says: “Let A be any K-algebra,” while def.alg.Kalg explicitly says its underlying structure is a “(noncommutative) ring.” In contrast, the elaborated target quantifies over `[inst_1 : CommRing A]`, inherited from the body/signature of `FPS.polyEval`, which requires `[CommRing A]`. Thus the theorem proves the evaluation formula only for commutative target algebras, omitting the genuinely noncommutative algebras covered by the informal statement. The displayed summand `(algebraMap K A) (f.coeff n) * a ^ n` otherwise correctly encodes the blueprint’s scalar product `f_n · a^n`, and `f.support` correctly indexes the nonzero coefficients.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint allows any K-algebra, whose underlying ring may be noncommutative, whereas the target assumes A is a commutative ring. For an arbitrary possibly noncommutative K-algebra, the same identity follows directly from the evaluation definition: f[1] = ∑ₙ (algebraMap K A)(fₙ) · 1ⁿ, and 1ⁿ = 1, so this is the image in A of the finite sum of the coefficients. This is a routine generalization requiring no use of commutativity in A.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pol.eva.justification: The informal statement says “any K-algebra A,” and `def.alg.Kalg` explicitly says its underlying structure is a “(noncommutative) ring.” The elaborated target instead binds `[inst_1 : CommRing A]`. Apart from this unnecessary restriction, `FPS.polyEval f 1` unfolds to `Polynomial.aeval 1 f`, matching the defined evaluation f[1], while `f.sum fun x c => c` is the support-finite sum of all coefficients and `(algebraMap K A)` implements their coercion into A.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint quantifies over any K-algebra, whose underlying ring may be noncommutative. The formal theorem can only be instantiated when A is a commutative ring. Recovering the blueprint requires proving the same finite evaluation formula for an arbitrary, potentially noncommutative K-algebra; the stated theorem cannot supply that case, so this requires a new generalization carrying essentially the theorem's proof.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pol.eva.justification: The informal definition says, “Let A be any K-algebra,” and defines a K-algebra using a “(noncommutative) ring.” In contrast, the elaborated signature assumes `[inst_1 : CommRing A]`. Thus the formal declaration omits all noncommutative K-algebras covered by the blueprint. The remaining formula agrees: `FPS.polyEval f a` unfolds to `Polynomial.aeval a f`, and the right side sums `(algebraMap K A) (f.coeff n) * a ^ n` over `Finset.range (f.natDegree + 1)`, i.e. indices from 0 through the natural degree.

discrepancies.bridge: To recover the blueprint, one must generalize evaluation and the zero-evaluation theorem to an arbitrary, potentially noncommutative, ring A with an Algebra K A structure, for example directly using Polynomial.aeval. The stated theorem cannot be instantiated for such an A, so it supplies no proof for the cases it excludes; a separate generalized theorem is required.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pol.eva.justification: The blueprint quantifies over “any K-algebra A,” while its definition says that A is a “(noncommutative) ring.” In contrast, the elaborated target requires `[inst_1 : CommRing A]`, inherited by `FPS.polyEval`, whose definition likewise has `[CommRing A]`. Thus the formal theorem proves the identity only for commutative target algebras. Its conclusion, `FPS.polyEval f 0 = (algebraMap K A) (f.coeff 0)`, otherwise correctly expresses that evaluation at zero equals the constant coefficient coerced into A, but it does not certify the claimed noncommutative cases.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.prod.fa.justification: Both formal conclusions exactly encode the two blueprint factorizations using zero-based `Fin` indices. The first asserts `∏ i ∈ P, A (σ i) i = ∏ j, A (Q.orderEmbOfFin … (extractAlpha … j)) (P.orderEmbOfFin … j)`, which unfolds to `∏_{i∈P} A_{σ(i),i} = ∏_j A_{q_{α(j)},p_j}` because `orderEmbOfFin` enumerates each finset increasingly and `extractAlpha` is defined by `σ(p_j)=q_{α(j)}`. The second similarly asserts `∏ i ∈ Pᶜ, B (σ i) i = ∏ j, B (Qᶜ.orderEmbOfFin … (extractBeta … j)) (Pᶜ.orderEmbOfFin … j)`, exactly matching the claimed complementary product with `p'_j`, `q'_j`, and `β`. The hypotheses `P.card = Q.card` and `imageFinset σ P = Q` match `|P|=|Q|` and `σ(P)=Q`; the `CommRing R` setting supplies the commutative finite products and is compatible with the claim.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.qbinomi.justification: The formal signature exactly matches the blueprint: `[CommRing L]`, `[Ring A]`, and `[Algebra L A]` encode “Let A be an L-algebra”; `(ω : L) (a b : A)` matches the chosen elements; the hypothesis `b * a = ω • (a * b)` is precisely `ba = ω · ab`; and `∀ (k : ℕ), b * a ^ k = ω ^ k • (a ^ k * b)` is precisely the claimed identity for every natural number k. The scalar action `•` is the algebra’s action of L on A, as required.

discrepancies.bridge: One must prove that the recursively defined function with boundary values `qBinomial q n 0 = 1`, `qBinomial q 0 (k+1) = 0` and recurrence `qBinomial q (n+1) (k+1) = qBinomial q n k + q^(k+1) * qBinomial q n (k+1)` equals the blueprint's generating function over partitions whose largest part is at most `n-k` and whose length is at most `k`. This requires a substantive q-Pascal/partition decomposition or an equivalent weighted bijection, rather than mere unfolding or notational re-encoding.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.qbinomi.justification: The formal right-hand side uses `AlgebraicCombinatorics.QBinomialRec.qBinomial q n k`, whose body is the displayed well-founded recursion, especially the branch `x.1 k + q ^ (k + 1) * x.1 (k + 1)`. In contrast, the blueprint fixes `\binom n k_q` by the explicit partition sum `\sum_{\lambda ... \text{largest part}\le n-k,\ \text{length}\le k} q^{|\lambda|}`. The project docstring says these definitions are equivalent, but its claim and the referenced equivalence theorem do not replace the supplied recursive body. Establishing that equivalence carries substantial combinatorial content. Apart from this dependency mismatch, `Finset.range n`, its powerset filtered by `S.card = k`, the exponent `∑ i ∈ S, i`, and `k * (k - 1) / 2` match the subset-sum formula.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint fixes only a commutative ring K, so its claim includes rings with zero divisors. The formal theorem can be instantiated only when `[IsDomain R]` holds. Recovering the blueprint requires a new proof that the staircase alternant is regular over every commutative coefficient ring—for example, by identifying it with the Vandermonde product and proving its factors, hence their product, are non-zero-divisors over an arbitrary ring. This is substantive and is not supplied by the domain-restricted theorem.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.sf.arho.justification: The informal setting says “Fix a commutative ring K” and the statement claims “The element a_ρ of the polynomial ring P is regular,” without an integral-domain assumption. In contrast, the elaborated signature is `∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing R] {N : ℕ} [IsDomain R], IsRegular ...`. Thus the formal theorem covers only integral domains and does not certify the claim for arbitrary commutative rings. The remaining encodings agree: `rho N i = N - 1 - ↑i` represents `(N-1,N-2,…,0)`, and the sum defining `alternant` matches the determinant expansion up to the routine finite-index re-encoding. Lean's two-sided `IsRegular` is stronger than the informal one-sided zero-kernel condition and therefore does certify that part in the commutative polynomial ring.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.sf.cont.justification: The formal conclusion is exactly the required monotonicity inequality: `contentColGeq T (j + 1) i ≤ contentColGeq T j i`. The dependency describes `contentColGeq T j i` as counting occurrences of `i` in columns `j` and beyond, matching `cont(col_{≥ j} T)_i`. The formal theorem quantifies over every `j : ℕ`, whereas the blueprint only requires positive integers, so it is strictly more general. Likewise, arbitrary `lam mu : Fin N → ℕ` include the blueprint’s nested `N`-partitions as a special case. `Tableau lam mu` is a map from the 1-indexed skew diagram to `Fin N`, matching a filling by the `N` possible entries up to the standard finite-index encoding.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.shift.e.justification: The two formal theorems exactly realize the two enumerated conclusions. `extractAlpha_leftShift_eq` proves `↑(Equiv.Perm.sign (extractAlpha P' Q ... σ' ...)) = ↑(Equiv.Perm.sign (extractAlpha P Q ... σ ...))`, matching `$(-1)^{\alpha_{\sigma'}}=(-1)^{\alpha_\sigma}$`; `extractBeta_leftShift_eq` gives the analogous equality for `β`. The bodies of `extractAlpha` and `extractBeta` use the increasing enumerations of `P,Q` and their complements exactly as specified by the informal extraction definition. The formal assignments `P' := imageFinset (Equiv.swap i ⟨↑i+1,hi⟩) P` and `σ' := σ * s` match `$P'=s_i(P)$` and `$\sigma'=\sigma\cdot s_i$`, with multiplication acting right factor first. The hypotheses `hi_notP : i ∉ P` and `hiplus_P : ⟨↑i+1,hi⟩ ∈ P` unpack the stated left-shift situation, while `hi : ↑i+1<n` is precisely the zero-based encoding of a valid simple transposition. Coercing `Equiv.Perm.sign` from `ℤˣ` to `ℤ` yields the informal integer-valued sign.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.shift.i.justification: The formal implication exactly matches the blueprint’s direction: the hypothesis is the sign decomposition formula for `(P', Q, σ')`, and the conclusion is the same formula for `(P, Q, σ)`. The formal definitions agree with the parenthetical specification: `s := Equiv.swap i ⟨↑i + 1, hi⟩`, `P' := imageFinset s P`, and `σ' := σ * s`, matching “where $P' = s_i(P)$, $\sigma' = \sigma \cdot s_i$.” The assumptions `i ∉ P` and `⟨↑i + 1, hi⟩ ∈ P` encode that this adjacent swap is a left shift, while `hcard : P.card = Q.card` and `hσ : imageFinset σ P = Q` are the domain conditions needed for the displayed sign decomposition and its extracted permutations. The supplied convention confirms that permutation multiplication sends `x` to `σ (s x)`, exactly as required.

discrepancies.bridge: The formal hypothesis assumes summability over every dependent pair `(i,k) : Σ i, S i`, including all terms with `k = 0`, whereas the blueprint assumes it only over `\overline S = {(i,k) : k ≠ 0}`. To recover the blueprint claim, define `q i k = 0` when `k = 0` and `q i k = p i k` otherwise. The blueprint hypothesis gives summability of `q` over the full sigma type by extension by zero. Apply the formal theorem to `q`; for each fixed `i`, this gives summability away from zero, and replacing the single zero term by `p i 0` preserves summability. These are routine reindexing and finite-modification steps.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.fib.gf.justification: The decisive formal fragment is `(PowerSeries.mk fun n => ↑(AlgebraicCombinatorics.FPS.fibonacci n))`, while the blueprint requires `F(x) = ∑_{n≥0} f_n x^n`. The package supplies neither the body nor a characterization/docstring of `PowerSeries.mk`, so it is unavailable whether this term is the formal power series whose nth coefficient is `↑(fibonacci n)`. A reference establishing, for example, that the nth coefficient of `PowerSeries.mk a` is `a n`, is needed to determine faithfulness. The supplied definition `fibonacci := Nat.fib` does match the blueprint’s Fibonacci recurrence, and the RHS has the expected form `X * (1 - X - X^2)⁻¹`, but the missing meaning of `PowerSeries.mk` prevents verifying the generating-function side.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.fps.lau.justification: The available signatures certify the structural and invertibility conclusions: `laurentSeries_commRing` has type `CommRing (LaurentSeries K)`, `laurentSeries_algebra` has type `Algebra K (LaurentSeries K)`, and `LaurentSeries_X_isUnit` asserts `IsUnit ((HahnSeries.single 1) 1)`, matching “a commutative K-algebra” and “The element x is invertible.” Also, `LaurentSeries R` unfolds to `HahnSeries ℤ R`, consistent with the blueprint’s stated Mathlib representation. However, the blueprint additionally fixes the operations concretely: `c_n = ∑_{i∈ℤ} a_i b_{n-i}`, inherited entrywise module operations, and unity `(δ_{i,0})`. The relevant formal bodies are only `fun {K} [CommRing K] => inferInstance`; the supplied Hahn-series instance chain omits the multiplication, scalar-action, and one implementations behind `⋯` or unavailable dependencies. Thus the package does not determine whether those concrete operations and their well-definedness agree with the blueprint. A coefficient formula for Hahn-series multiplication and lemmas/bodies identifying scalar multiplication and `1` coefficientwise would be needed to decide faithfulness.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.fps.lim.justification: The decisive formal conclusion is `PowerSeries.CoeffStabilizesTo f (PowerSeries.mk g)`, while the blueprint concludes stabilization to `∑_{n∈ℕ} g_n x^n`, defined as the FPS whose `n`th coefficient is `g_n`. Determining equivalence therefore requires knowing that `(PowerSeries.coeff n) (PowerSeries.mk g) = g n`. The package provides neither the signature/body/docstring of `PowerSeries.mk` nor a coefficient-of-`mk` theorem, and absent library material cannot be assumed. Thus the meaning of the formal limit is underdetermined from the supplied material.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint assumes only that the partial products have a coefficientwise-stabilizing limit. It does not require every factor to have constant coefficient 1. That condition cannot be derived from convergence: over ℤ, take f₀ to be the constant FPS 2 and fᵢ = 1 for i > 0. Every partial product is 2, so the limit exists, but constantCoeff (f₀) ≠ 1. Recovering the blueprint theorem would therefore require a genuinely more general proof handling factors with non-unit constant terms (including finite exceptional factors), rather than an application of either formal target.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.fps.lim.justification: Both targets add the hypothesis `(hconst : ∀ (i : ℕ), PowerSeries.constantCoeff (f i) = 1)`, whereas the blueprint says only: “such that lim_{i→∞} ∏_{n=0}^{i} f_n exists.” This restriction is substantive because `PowerSeries.IsMultipliable` unfolds to a predicate whose first conjunct is exactly `∀ i, constantCoeff (f i) = 1`, while the informal `multipliable` means that every product coefficient is finitely determined and permits, for example, finitely many factors with constant coefficient different from 1. Thus the two formal declarations prove the desired product identity and multipliability only for a restricted normalized class and do not certify the unrestricted blueprint statement.

The formal hypothesis `hf : PowerSeries.IsSummable f` unfolds to `∀ n, {i | (PowerSeries.coeff n) (f i) ≠ 0}.Finite`, exactly matching the blueprint’s requirement that for every coefficient, all but finitely many terms have zero coefficient. The sequence in the conclusion, `fun i => ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (i + 1), f j`, is precisely the partial sum from `0` through `i`, since `Finset.range (i + 1)` contains exactly the naturals less than `i + 1`. The conclusion unfolds through `PowerSeries.CoeffStabilizesTo` and `Seq.StabilizesTo` to coefficientwise eventual equality with `PowerSeries.tsum' f hf`. Finally, `PowerSeries.tsum'` constructs the FPS whose `n`-th coefficient is the finite sum over the nonzero `n`-th coefficients, matching the blueprint’s definition of the essentially finite infinite sum. Thus the theorem directly certifies `lim_{i→∞} ∑_{n=0}^i f_n = ∑_{n∈ℕ} f_n` under the stated notion of limit.

discrepancies.bridge: The blueprint does not assume that K is a commutative ring, while both formal declarations quantify only over K equipped with CommRing. Recovering the unrestricted blueprint would require proving the implication for every coefficient setting intended by its definitions, and that implication is not generally valid without additive cancellation: in an idempotent coefficient semiring, infinitely many identical nonzero coefficients can have stabilizing partial sums while failing the stated finite-support summability condition. Thus the omitted algebraic hypothesis cannot be discharged routinely.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.fps.lim.justification: Both elaborated signatures begin with `∀ {K : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing K]`, whereas the informal statement only says “a sequence of FPSs” and the supplied informal definitions refer to FPSs “over K” without imposing commutative-ring axioms on K. Apart from this restriction, the two declarations jointly match the two conclusions: `PowerSeries.IsSummable f` formalizes “the family ... is summable,” and `PowerSeries.tsum' f ⋯ = lim` formalizes `∑ f_n = lim ...`; `Finset.range (i + 1)` is exactly the index set from 0 through i, and `CoeffStabilizesTo` unfolds to the supplied coefficientwise notion of convergence.

discrepancies.bridge: To recover the blueprint, one must generalize evaluation from commutative coefficient algebras to arbitrary, potentially noncommutative K-algebras and prove all seven identities there. The supplied `Polynomial.aeval` can represent evaluation into a merely `Semiring A` with `Algebra K A`, but `FPS.polyEval` and consequently every target require `CommRing A`. The missing noncommutative cases cannot be obtained by specializing these theorems; they require a generalized definition/theorem and new proofs.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.pol.eva.justification: Every target quantifies over `[inst_1 : CommRing A]`, inherited from `FPS.polyEval`, whose signature likewise contains `[inst_1 : CommRing A]`. In contrast, the blueprint says “Let A be a K-algebra,” and its definition explicitly requires A to be “a (noncommutative) ring”; `def.alg.ring` removes multiplication commutativity. Thus the formal declarations establish (a)–(f) only for commutative A, omitting all genuinely noncommutative K-algebras allowed by the statement. The seven displayed equations otherwise match the blueprint: `FPS.polyEval` unfolds to `Polynomial.aeval`, `Polynomial.C` represents constants, `Polynomial.X` the indeterminate, and `Polynomial.comp` polynomial composition.

discrepancies.bridge: For an arbitrary ring A and q : A, first apply the formal theorem universally in the commutative polynomial ring ℤ[X] (with q = X), obtaining the corresponding polynomial identity. Evaluating that identity at q in A recovers the claimed equality. Integer coefficients commute with every element of a unital ring, and a routine induction shows that evaluation also transports the recurrence-based expression. Thus noncommutative rings are recoverable by a standard universal-polynomial reduction, without repeating the combinatorial proof.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.qbinomi.justification: The blueprint says “If a is any element of a ring A” and the theorem states the equality for a “ring element q,” whereas the elaborated signature quantifies only `∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing R] ...`. Hence the formal theorem cannot be instantiated directly for a noncommutative ring. Apart from that restriction, unfolding `qBinomialEval` and `qBinomialPolyDef` gives the stated sum over partitions (with the explicit zero case when `k > n`), while unfolding `qBinomial` gives the recurrence-based Gaussian coefficient, so the asserted equality matches the blueprint.

discrepancies.bridge: To recover part (b), one must prove algebraic independence and unique generation by h₁,…,h_N for arbitrary commutative rings with zero divisors, which the formal theorems exclude. This requires establishing bijectivity of the evaluation map over general commutative rings, for example through universal Newton–Girard identities and the elementary-symmetric equivalence; it is a substantive extension, not a routine instance discharge.

To recover part (c), one must remove the domain hypothesis and prove that evaluation at p₁,…,p_N is bijective for every commutative ℚ-algebra, including those with zero divisors. The supplied formal results do not cover these rings; extending them requires a substantive argument using Newton identities and invertibility of positive integers in a ℚ-algebra.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.sf.ftsf.justification: Part (a) is faithfully covered: `esymm_algebraicIndependent` assumes only `[CommRing K]`, `esymm_generates_symmetric` gives `∃! g`, and `esymmAlgEquiv'` directly supplies the stated K-algebra isomorphism. Part (b), however, is stated in the blueprint under “Fix a commutative ring K,” while both h-targets require `[IsDomain K]`. Part (c) says only “assume that K is a commutative ℚ-algebra,” whereas both power-sum targets require `[Algebra ℚ K] [IsDomain K]`. Thus the formal package omits the claimed h- and p-results for commutative rings or ℚ-algebras with zero divisors.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.sf.pier.justification: The supplied informal material does not define the notation `s_μ` or `s_λ`, nor does it define the ambient ring `𝒮`. By contrast, the formal targets use `SymmetricFunctions.schur`, whose body is `fun ... lam => ∑ T ∈ SymmetricFunctions.ssytFinset lam, T.toMonomial`, in `MvPolynomial (Fin N) R` for arbitrary `[CommRing R]`. Thus the package does not establish that this SSYT generating polynomial is the object denoted by `s_λ` in the informal equations `h_n s_μ = ... s_λ` and `e_n s_μ = ... s_λ`. The supplied definitions of `MvPolynomial.hsymm`/`esymm` and of the horizontal/vertical strip finsets otherwise match the informal definitions. A blueprint definition of Schur polynomials and of the ambient symmetric-polynomial ring is needed for a decisive verdict.
